title: Ang 133–136: the twelve months
hook: Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, then the day and night hymn
tomorrow: what's the one thing that's never yours to take?

segments.voice: Yesterday, closing hymns: a jewel kept hidden, and a Word that shows it. Both sides, one verse. Today, the calendar.

The first cold morning. A heater clicking on after months off, and that smell of dust burning away. Leaves in the gutter, a hoodie you haven't worn since spring. Every month has its own feel on the skin. So what is this month asking of you? Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, on ang 133, walks the twelve months of the Punjabi year and gives each one a question of its own.
screen: `THE FIRST COLD MORNING.` → `EVERY MONTH HAS A FEEL.` → `TWELVE MONTHS, TWELVE QUESTIONS.`

segments.voice: Barah Maha means the twelve months, and Guru Arjan's begins with Chet, at spring. In paraphrase: in Chet, remember the Lord of the universe, and deep joy comes. Then the year turns, month by month, each verse with its weather and its longing. Here's the one for autumn, Kattak, in paraphrase: in Kattak, do good deeds; don't put the blame on anyone else. A month for clean hands. And here's the one for the cold, Poh, in paraphrase: in Poh, the frost doesn't touch the one the Lord holds close. You can feel that one in your shoulders. The poem doesn't ask you to escape the season. It asks you to meet the One inside it: joy in the spring air, honesty in the harvest, warmth in the frost. After the months, on ang 136, comes a hymn of day and night, the same idea at a smaller scale: every hour can hold remembrance. Some Sikhs hear the month's verse read at the gurdwara as each new month begins. Your month has a verse, and a feel on the skin to go with it.
screen: `CHET: REMEMBER, AND JOY COMES.` · `KATTAK: GOOD DEEDS, NO BLAMING.` · `POH: THE FROST DOESN'T TOUCH YOU.` · `THEN DAY AND NIGHT.` · then, large: `YOUR MONTH.`

segments.voice: Step to a window or an open door, and give one slow minute to this month: the temperature on your skin, the light, the smell of the air. If you have the Barah Maha open, read your month's verse, then go back to the air. Let the season be the whole of the sit.
Ang 133. The page where Guru Arjan's Barah Maha begins, the twelve months, starting with Chet.
Carry it out the door: your month, and the question it brings. Whatever the weather, it's yours.

howItsDone: Some gurdwaras read the verse of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha for the new month on its first day, called sangrand, and some Sikh families read it at home as the month turns.

fork.setup: a group project tanks. it's autumn, and everyone is pointing at someone else. you've read the Kattak verse. what does it ask of you?
options: do your own good work and put the blame on no one else.
figure out who really caused it, then say so, fairly.
stay out of it; seasons pass and so will this.
fork.reveal: in Kattak, Guru Arjan says: do good deeds, don't put the blame on anyone else. a month for clean hands.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape senses (weather on the skin carries the idea; the practice is a minute at a window with this month's air).
Chet (ang 133), Kattak and Poh (ang 135) verses paraphrased. Confirm Angs and wording. 'Twelve months' is in the title Barah Maha itself.
Kattak called 'autumn' and Poh 'cold winter' month: general seasonal descriptions of the Punjabi calendar, no dates given. Confirm.
The day-and-night hymn on ang 136 (Din Raini) is only named and summarized as 'every hour can hold remembrance'; confirm the summary.
howItsDone and teach: reading the month's Barah Maha verse on sangrand at 'some' gurdwaras. Sangrand observance is debated among Sikhs; the lesson only says some do it. Confirm the framing is fair.
Gurmukhi month names ਚੇਤ, ਕੱਤਕ, ਪੋਹ are modern Punjabi spellings (the Granth has ਚੇਤਿ, ਕਤਿਕਿ, ਪੋਖਿ); confirm or swap.
v3 storyline: Bebe's weekly appearance; she pulls the last of her chilies and quotes the Kattak verse after Simran blames a driver for her own mistake.
